candidates.workingClaim: October 9, 1874: On October 9, 1874, representatives of 22 countries meeting in Bern signed the Treaty of Bern, founding the organization now known as the Universal Postal Union. The anniversary is marked around the world today as World Post Day.

October 9, 1604: On October 9, 1604, Italian astronomer Lodovico delle Colombo first observed a bright new star in the constellation Ophiuchus. Johannes Kepler, working in Prague, began observing it on October 17, and the stellar explosion is now known by his name.

October 9, 1888: On October 9, 1888, the Washington Monument in Washington, D.C., opened to the public after a steam elevator was installed. The obelisk had been completed in 1884 and dedicated in February 1885.
October 9, 1962: On October 9, 1962, Uganda gained independence from Britain. Milton Obote became prime minister at the head of a coalition between the Uganda People's Congress and Kabaka Yekka.

October 9, 1967: On October 9, 1967, the revolutionary Ernesto "Che" Guevara was executed at La Higuera in Bolivia, a day after a U.S.-trained Bolivian army unit captured him. Declassified records show CIA involvement in the campaign against his guerrilla group.

October 10, 1911: On October 10, 1911, an uprising broke out in Wuchang, part of present-day Wuhan in central China. It triggered the Xinhai Revolution, which overthrew the Qing dynasty and founded a republic, and the date is still commemorated as Double Ten.
October 10, 1970: On October 10, 1970, Fiji became independent with dominion status. The date echoed October 10, 1874, when Fiji had been ceded to Great Britain.

October 10, 1868: On October 10, 1868, planter Carlos Manuel de Cespedes proclaimed Cuban independence at his La Demajagua plantation near Bayamo, launching the Ten Years' War against Spanish rule. He freed his enslaved workers, who joined his rebel force.

October 10, 1967: On October 10, 1967, the Outer Space Treaty entered into force. Formally governing the exploration and use of outer space, the Moon, and other celestial bodies, it remains the foundation of international space law.

October 10, 1845: On October 10, 1845, the Naval School opened at Fort Severn in Annapolis, Maryland, with 50 midshipmen and seven professors. Established through the efforts of Navy Secretary George Bancroft, it became the United States Naval Academy in 1850.
October 11, 1968: On October 11, 1968, Apollo 7 lifted off from Cape Kennedy with Walter Schirra, Donn Eisele, and Walter Cunningham aboard. It was the first Apollo mission to carry a crew.
October 11, 1962: On October 11, 1962, the Second Vatican Council opened in Rome. Announced by Pope John XXIII, the council met in sessions until December 8, 1965.
October 11, 1899: On October 11, 1899, the South African War, also called the Second Boer War, began between Britain and the Boer republics. The conflict lasted until May 31, 1902.

October 11, 1982: On October 11, 1982, the hull of the Mary Rose, Henry VIII's warship that sank in 1545, was raised from the seabed of the Solent after many years of searching, excavation, and recording.
October 12, 1968: On October 12, 1968, Equatorial Guinea gained independence from Spain.
October 13, 2010: On October 13, 2010, rescuers began lifting 33 miners out of the San Jose gold and copper mine in northern Chile, 69 days after a collapse trapped them underground.
October 14, 1066: On October 14, 1066, William, duke of Normandy, defeated King Harold II of England at the Battle of Hastings. The victory established the Normans as the rulers of England.

October 14, 1947: On October 14, 1947, U.S. Air Force pilot Chuck Yeager flew the Bell X-1 faster than the speed of sound over Rogers Dry Lake in California. The achievement was kept secret until June 1948.

October 14, 1806: On October 14, 1806, Napoleon's forces defeated the armies of Prussia and Saxony in twin battles at Jena and Auerstedt. The victories let Napoleon complete his conquest of Prussia within six weeks.
October 15, 2003: On October 15, 2003, Shenzhou 5 carried Yang Liwei, China's first astronaut, into orbit on a 21-hour spaceflight.
October 15, 1997: On October 15, 1997, NASA's Cassini spacecraft launched on its long journey to Saturn, where it would study the planet, its rings, and its moons.

October 12, 1810: On October 12, 1810, the festival that became Oktoberfest began in Munich, celebrating the marriage of the Bavarian crown prince, later King Louis I, to Princess Therese von Sachsen-Hildburghausen.

October 12, 1492: On October 12, 1492, land was sighted from the Pinta, ending the Atlantic crossing of Christopher Columbus's fleet, which had left Spain on August 3. The island, called Guanahani, is usually identified with San Salvador in the Bahamas, though the exact site is disputed.

October 12, 1964: On October 12, 1964, Voskhod 1 carried commander Vladimir Komarov, engineer Konstantin Feoktistov, and doctor Boris Yegorov into Earth orbit. It was the first spacecraft to carry more than one person, and Yegorov became the first doctor in space.

October 13, 1307: On October 13, 1307, King Philip IV of France ordered the arrest of every Templar in France and seized the order's property there. The arrests made much of Europe aware of the crimes alleged against the order.

October 13, 1792: On October 13, 1792, construction of the White House officially began with the laying of a cornerstone during a Masonic ceremony. Enslaved people worked alongside hired laborers at every stage of construction through 1800.

October 13, 1943: On October 13, 1943, Italy declared war on Germany. Marshal Pietro Badoglio read the declaration at Brindisi, and the document, signed by King Victor Emmanuel III, was sent to Berlin through the Italian Embassy in Madrid.

October 14, 1962: On October 14, 1962, an American U-2 flight over Cuba took photographs that analysts studied over the following days. The images showed the Soviet Union building nuclear missile bases in Cuba, bringing the two superpowers into direct nuclear confrontation.

October 15, 1582: On October 15, 1582, the Gregorian calendar took effect. Proclaimed by Pope Gregory XIII to reform the Julian calendar, the change advanced the calendar by 10 days, so the day after October 4 was counted as October 15.
October 15, 1997: On October 15, 1997, ThrustSSC set the world land speed record at 763 mph, becoming the first land vehicle to officially break the sound barrier.

October 9, 1963: On October 9, 1963, an estimated 260 million cubic metres of rock broke free from Monte Toc and fell into the reservoir behind the Vaiont Dam in Italy. The slide sent a wave 150 to 200 metres above the dam, over its crest and down the narrow valley below. The town of Longarone, almost directly below the dam, was nearly completely destroyed, and about 2,000 people died. The dam itself was largely unaffected and still stands, but its reservoir has never been refilled.

October 9, 2012: On October 9, 2012, Malala Yousafzai was shot in the head by a gunman from the Tehreek-e Taliban Pakistan (TTP) as she was travelling home from school. Under the name Gul Makai, she had written a diary for BBC Urdu about daily life as the group restricted girls' schooling in Pakistan. She survived after treatment in Birmingham, England, and continued her campaign for girls' education. In 2014, at 17, she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, becoming the youngest Nobel laureate at the time.

October 9, 2004: On October 9, 2004, Afghans voted for a president under a new constitution, approved that January, which called for a directly elected head of state. Hamid Karzai, who had led the interim administration since late December 2001, won more than 55 percent of an estimated eight million votes. More than 40 percent of the voters were women. The United States congratulated Karzai as Afghanistan's first democratically elected leader, and he was sworn into office later that year.

October 10, 1964: On October 10, 1964, the Summer Olympic Games opened in Tokyo, the first time the Olympics were held in Asia. More than 5,000 athletes from 93 countries competed until October 24. The Tokyo Games added volleyball and judo to the programme and were the first to use computers to keep statistics. South Africa did not take part, having been banned by the IOC for its policy of apartheid.

October 10, 1973: On October 10, 1973, Spiro T. Agnew resigned as vice president of the United States. He pleaded nolo contendere (no contest) to a single federal count of failing to report $29,500 of income he had received in 1967, and he was fined $10,000 and sentenced to three years of unsupervised probation. He was the second person to resign the vice presidency. The first, John C. Calhoun, had stepped down in 1832.

October 10, 1963: On October 10, 1963, the treaty banning nuclear weapons tests in the atmosphere, in outer space and underwater entered into force. The United States, the Soviet Union and the United Kingdom had signed it in Moscow on August 5, and the U.S. Senate had ratified it on September 24. The treaty still allowed underground tests and set up no inspection system. More than 100 other governments signed within a few months, with France and China the notable exceptions. It did not reduce nuclear stockpiles or halt the production of nuclear weapons.

October 10, 1846: On October 10, 1846, the British astronomer William Lassell discovered Triton, just 17 days after the planet Neptune itself had been found. Triton is about 2,700 kilometres (1,680 miles) across. It is the only large moon in the solar system that orbits in the opposite direction to its planet's rotation. When Voyager 2 flew past in 1989, it found active geysers and surface temperatures of about -235°C (-391°F), among the coldest in the solar system.

October 10, 2010: On October 10, 2010, a constitutional reform of the Kingdom of the Netherlands dissolved the Netherlands Antilles, a grouping of five Caribbean islands. Curaçao and Sint Maarten became autonomous countries within the kingdom, while Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba became public entities of the Netherlands itself. Aruba had already left the Netherlands Antilles in 1986. Since 2010 the kingdom has consisted of four countries: the Netherlands, Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten.

October 11, 1984: On October 11, 1984, during the Space Shuttle Challenger's STS-41G mission, Kathryn D. Sullivan became the first American woman to walk in space. With fellow astronaut David C. Leestma, she spent three hours and 29 minutes outside the shuttle, where Leestma showed that satellites could be refuelled in orbit and Sullivan stowed a malfunctioning antenna. She was not the first woman to do so: the Soviet cosmonaut Svetlana Savitskaya had walked in space that July. Sullivan later led the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and in 2020 she became the first woman to descend to the Challenger Deep, the deepest point in the ocean.

October 11, 1975: On October 11, 1975, NBC broadcast the first episode of what became Saturday Night Live, hosted by the comedian George Carlin. Instead of acting in sketches, Carlin performed four stand-up monologues, between music from Billy Preston and Janis Ian and a short film by Albert Brooks. The show was created by Lorne Michaels with Dick Ebersol, and its first cast, the "Not Ready for Primetime Players," included Dan Aykroyd, John Belushi, Chevy Chase, Jane Curtin, Garrett Morris, Laraine Newman and Gilda Radner. It became one of the longest-running programs in television and has won 90 Emmys.

October 11, 1991: On October 11, 1991, the law professor Anita Hill testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee that Supreme Court nominee Clarence Thomas had made unwanted sexual advances and lewd comments when she worked for him. She faced a panel of 14 male senators, led by Joe Biden, and skeptical, often hostile questioning. Thomas was narrowly confirmed, 52 to 48. The hearings raised public awareness of sexual harassment at work, and in the 1992 "Year of the Woman" the number of women in Congress roughly doubled.

October 11, 1910: On October 11, 1910, former president Theodore Roosevelt went up with the aviator Archibald Hoxsey during the International Aviation Meet at Kinloch Field outside St. Louis, Missouri. The two men circled the airfield twice in "three minutes and twenty seconds." Roosevelt was no longer in office, so the first president to fly was a former one. Franklin D. Roosevelt later became the first sitting president to travel by airplane.

October 12, 2000: On October 12, 2000, suicide bombers steered a small boat into the side of the U.S. Navy destroyer USS Cole in the harbour of Aden, Yemen. The explosion killed 17 sailors and wounded 39. The attackers were militants associated with al-Qaeda. The damaged ship was later carried away aboard the heavy transport ship MV Blue Marlin.

October 12, 2002: At about 11 p.m. on October 12, 2002, bombs exploded at Paddy's pub and outside the Sari Club on Jalan Legian in Bali, Indonesia, and a third went off near the U.S. consulate. The attacks killed 202 people, including 88 Australians. They were carried out by Jemaah Islamiah, a Southeast Asian militant group inspired by and linked to al-Qaeda.

October 12, 1915: On October 12, 1915, the British nurse Edith Cavell was shot by a German firing squad in Brussels, together with Philippe Baucq. As matron of the Berkendael Institute, she had joined an underground network that helped British, French and Belgian soldiers reach the Netherlands, and about 200 men had been aided before her arrest in August 1915. Her court-martial was considered legally valid, but the Allies publicised her execution widely, and it caused outrage abroad.

October 12, 1999: On October 12, 1999, Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif dismissed the army chief, General Pervez Musharraf, while Musharraf was out of the country, and tried to stop the plane carrying him home from landing at Karachi airport. The armed forces took control of the airport and other government installations and deposed Sharif. Musharraf headed the military government that followed and took the presidency in early 2001. He announced his resignation in August 2008.

October 13, 1775: On October 13, 1775, the Continental Congress voted to fit out ships for the war against Britain. A Marine Committee, appointed later, sent the first Continental squadron to sea under the command of Esek Hopkins, with orders to capture munitions.

October 13, 1903: On October 13, 1903, the Boston Americans beat the Pittsburgh Pirates 3-0 at Boston's Huntington Avenue Grounds to win the first modern World Series, five games to three. Pitcher Bill Dinneen allowed only four hits and ended the game by striking out Honus Wagner. The best-of-nine series between the American League and National League champions drew just over 100,000 fans, and each player's share of the receipts was slightly more than $1,000.

October 13, 1972: On October 13, 1972, a Uruguayan Air Force plane carrying the Old Christians rugby team and others, 45 people in all, crashed high in the Andes. More than two months later, two of the survivors, Roberto Canessa and Nando Parrado, trekked across the mountains for nine days until Parrado spotted horsemen across a river. He threw a note tied to a rock to a Chilean muleteer, Sergio Catalán, who alerted the authorities. By December 23, 1972, 16 men had been rescued.

October 13, 1988: On October 13, 1988, Cardinal Anastasio Ballestrero of Turin announced that radiocarbon tests had dated the Shroud of Turin, with 95 percent certainty, to between 1260 and 1390. Laboratories at Oxford University, the University of Arizona and the Federal Institute of Technology in Zurich had each tested samples of the cloth. The Vatican encouraged further scientific study and said Christians could continue to venerate the shroud as an image of Christ. The Holy See has made no official pronouncement on whether it is authentic.

October 13, 54: On October 13, 54 CE, the Roman emperor Claudius died and was succeeded by Nero. Claudius had married his niece Agrippina and adopted her son, the future Nero, to the disadvantage of his own son Britannicus. Roman tradition is unanimous that Agrippina poisoned Claudius, though the accounts differ on the details.

October 14, 1912: On October 14, 1912, Theodore Roosevelt was shot outside the Hotel Gilpatrick in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, by John Flammang Schrank. The bullet was slowed by the folded 50-page manuscript of his speech and his eyeglass case before lodging in his chest wall. Roosevelt went on to speak for about 80 minutes, telling the audience, "it takes more than that to kill a bull moose." Doctors decided not to remove the bullet, and he carried it for the rest of his life.

October 14, 1943: On October 14, 1943, prisoners at Sobibor, a German killing center, rose up. Led by Leon Feldhendler and Aleksandr (Sasha) Pechersky, they killed 11 German personnel and several guards, and about 300 of the roughly 600 prisoners still in the camp broke out. About 100 were caught in the manhunt that followed, and some 50 escapees survived the war. The Germans then dismantled the camp, where at least 167,000 people had been killed since April 1942.

October 14, 1926: On October 14, 1926, A. A. Milne's Winnie-the-Pooh was first published, with illustrations by E. H. Shepard. Milne based the stories on the nursery toys and games of his son, Christopher Robin, who appears in the book with Pooh, Piglet, Eeyore and their friends. Their Hundred Acre Wood was modelled on Ashdown Forest in East Sussex, England. A second collection, The House at Pooh Corner, followed in 1928.

October 14, 1944: On October 14, 1944, the German field marshal Erwin Rommel died at Herrlingen, near Ulm, after taking poison. He had been implicated in the conspiracy against Hitler after the failed July Plot, and Hitler gave him the choice of taking poison, which would protect his family, or facing trial. Rommel had been nicknamed "the Desert Fox" for his surprise attacks while commanding the Afrika Korps in North Africa. After his death he was buried with full military honours.

October 15, 1917: On October 15, 1917, Margaretha Geertruida Zelle, the Dutch-born dancer known as Mata Hari, was executed by a French firing squad at Vincennes. A French military court had found her guilty that July of spying for Germany during World War I. She had taken German money as "agent H21" while also trying to work for France, but the investigating officer could not prove she had given the Germans useful information. Germany publicly cleared her in 1930, and French documents released in 2017 led many to see her as a scapegoat.

October 15, 1966: On October 15, 1966, the college students Huey P. Newton and Bobby Seale founded the Black Panther Party for Self-Defense in West Oakland, California. Its first aim was to patrol African American neighbourhoods to protect residents from police brutality. The party grew to more than 2,000 members with chapters in 48 states and ran community services such as the Free Breakfast for Children Program, begun in January 1969. FBI counterintelligence operations weakened it, and by the mid-1980s its activities had all but ceased.

October 15, 1951: On Monday evening, October 15, 1951, the first episode of I Love Lucy was broadcast, starring Lucille Ball and Desi Arnaz as a married couple, with Vivian Vance and William Frawley as their neighbours. Its 180 half-hour episodes were performed before a live studio audience and captured on film, which allowed them to be rerun and helped keep the series popular long after it ended.

October 15, 1815: On October 15, 1815, after nine weeks at sea aboard the Northumberland, Napoleon arrived at the island of St Helena, his place of exile after his defeat at Waterloo. Because his intended residence, Longwood, was not ready, he first lodged with the Balcombe family at a house called the Briars. He moved to Longwood on December 10, 1815. He died on May 5, 1821, at the age of 51.

October 15, 1987: On October 15, 1987, Thomas Sankara, the leader of Burkina Faso, was assassinated in Ouagadougou in a coup led by Blaise Compaoré. He was 37. On the first anniversary of his rise to power, in August 1984, Sankara had renamed Upper Volta as Burkina Faso, "land of upright people." His government fought corruption, promoted women's rights, education and health care, and planted 10 million trees against desertification. In 2022 Compaoré and nine others were convicted of complicity in his murder.
